message.content: {"criteria":[{"id":"C1","level":"Adequate","mark":7,"evidence":[{"where":"Introduction","quote":"Thus, only one satellite is required. This also just allows for simplicity in communications, reduces cost, and requires less time to build and launch."},{"where":"Introduction","quote":"The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education."}],"reasoning":"Primary mission, rationale, single-spacecraft justification and reef-monitoring need are clearly stated and motivated. Users are vague: operator is not clearly identified and customers are only generically named. Referencing is largely web links, with the Wikipedia source and broken entries weakening support. Strong at the top of Adequate, but not Accomplished."},{"id":"C2","level":"Adequate","mark":5,"evidence":[{"where":"Orbit","quote":"As the satellite can be launched directly into low-earth orbit, the only orbital manoeuvre occurs at the EOL segment of the satellite's mission."},{"where":"Launch","quote":"The proposed satellite will thus use the Vega E rocket as a launch vehicle"},{"where":"Orbit","quote":"the constant supply of sunlight to the satellite will be captured by solar panels"}],"reasoning":"Covers most required elements with STK access data, a Keplerian element table and inclination-altitude plot. However, the chosen launcher is unbuilt and contradicted by the launch-year text, the manoeuvre statements conflict with the no-thruster claim, and the constant-sunlight claim is wrong for a 600 km SSO. RAAN and ground-station selection are weakly justified, and no hand calculations or software files are shown."},{"id":"C3","level":"Adequate","mark":5,"evidence":[{"where":"Conclusion","quote":"A specific launch vehicle – the Vega E – has been selected although it has not been built yet."},{"where":"Conclusion","quote":"A polar sun-synchronous orbit allows for consistent illumination of the oceans while maintaining a constant sun angle."}],"reasoning":"Conclusions summarise the design and acknowledge launch-vehicle risk with a fallback (Vega C). They are largely restatements and generic, with no quantified outcomes or limitations on access or EOL, and they do not address the unresolved manoeuvre and EOL contradictions."},{"id":"C4","level":"Adequate","mark":4,"evidence":[{"where":"Mission Duration & EOL","quote":"It acts like a regular sail, utilising a large surface area to ‘ and is suitable for low-earth orbit altitudes [10]."},{"where":"Ground Control & Communications","quote":"for the purposed of this satellite"},{"where":"Bibliography","quote":"[5] f. https://www.qrg.northwestern.edu/"}],"reasoning":"Headings and a contents list give clear structure. Presentation is undermined by a truncated sentence, typos (purposed, complied, current owned), a duplicated access-table row, unnumbered figures and tables, and corrupted reference entries. Citation is inconsistent, with Wikipedia used as a source."},{"id":"R1","met":"yes","where":"Introduction"},{"id":"R2","met":"yes","where":"Mission Design"},{"id":"R3","met":"yes","where":"Introduction"},{"id":"R4","met":"yes","where":"Introduction"},{"id":"R5","met":"partial","where":"Introduction"},{"id":"R6","met":"partial","where":"Launch"},{"id":"R7","met":"yes","where":"Orbit"},{"id":"R8","met":"partial","where":"Orbit"},{"id":"R9","met":"partial","where":"Ground Control & Communications"},{"id":"R10","met":"partial","where":"Mission Duration & EOL"},{"id":"R11","met":"yes","where":"Ground Control & Communications"},{"id":"R12","met":"partial","where":"Orbit"},{"id":"R13","met":"yes","where":"Contents"},{"id":"R14","met":"partial","where":"Orbit"},{"id":"R15","met":"partial","where":"Bibliography"}],"technical_issues":[{"where":"Launch","issue":"Vega E is unbuilt and its launch date conflicts within the text (2024 first launch versus a 2025 mission), so the launch vehicle choice is not credible as stated."},{"where":"Orbit","issue":"The claim of constant sunlight for the satellite ignores eclipses in a 600 km sun-synchronous orbit, which affects power budget analysis."},{"where":"Orbit","issue":"RAAN precession is stated as 360° per year and 1° per day; the correct SSO rate is about 0.9856° per day. Also the RAAN initial value is linked to the launch site without justification."},{"where":"Orbit","issue":"Manoeuvre statements conflict: no orbital manoeuvres are said to be needed, yet the satellite is stated to be without thrusters, and the EOL section contradicts both."},{"where":"Ground Control & Communications","issue":"Claims near-polar orbit requires a polar ground station, then selects Mount Pleasant in Tasmania (about 43°S) without reconciling the reasoning or addressing link budget or antenna constraints."},{"where":"Ground Control & Communications","issue":"Access summary table duplicates row 14 as row 15 and the row labelled '----' is unclear, so the access statistics may be misreported."},{"where":"Mission Duration & EOL","issue":"Graveyard manoeuvre is described as requiring propulsion, and the drag sail discussion is truncated,

The latitude given for Kourou looks slightly off too, since it should be closer to 5.2°N than 5.05°N.

I'm checking the orbital parameters next: the 600 km sun-synchronous inclination looks right, but the RAAN starting value doesn't obviously match the launch site, and the daily precession rate is stated too loosely.

I'm checking the ground station choice and the access table next. The Tasmania site isn't polar, and the table seems to have a duplicated row and a missing one, so I'm looking at whether the mean access duration actually matches the listed values.

I'm checking the end-of-life plan now: the draft says the satellite will descend uncontrolled because that takes the least energy, but it also says a drag sail is needed, and that sentence cuts off mid-way. There's also a contradiction about whether any orbital manoeuvre happens at all, since the text both claims one at end of life and says the craft has no thrusters.

I'm going through the rest of the review notes, mostly the mission design and presentation: the missing hand calculations for the inclination, the perturbation claim in the executive summary that isn't backed up by the work, and the figure and table captions that are incomplete or missing.

I'm now going through the remaining referencing problems: a Wikipedia source used against the rubric, a broken entry, and a citation lifted from a spaceflight table without attribution. I'm also noting spelling and grammar slips, like "complied" and "purposed".

I'm scoring the introduction as covering the mission goal, the reason for it, and the number of spacecraft, though the users are only vaguely described and the sources are thin. Moving on to the main body, which has real evidence in the STK screenshots, access table, and orbital elements, but also several errors: the RAAN, the nonexistent Vega E, the conflicting manoeuvre claims, the broken drag-sail sentence, the Wikipedia source, the missing ground station rationale, and the "constant sunlight" mistake. I'm giving it a 5, and I'm now turning to the conclusion.

Now I'm scoring the presentation criterion, where the broken sentence, typos, duplicate table row, unlabelled figures and reference problems pull it down to a low-adequate mark. Next I'm going through the requirements one by one, marking the ones that are covered and noting that the operator is only vaguely identified.

I'm going through the remaining requirements against the draft, marking the ones that are only partly met, such as the ground station coverage, the end-of-life section with its broken sentence, the screenshots without the underlying software files, and the figures without numbers. The references are next to check, since the Wikipedia citation I already flagged is still in question.

I'm pulling out the wording of the sourcing problems now: a launch-efficiency claim cited to a source, the Wikipedia-style directory used as a reference, and the Vega E sentence that I'm planning to quote as evidence.

I'm checking the wording of the sourced claims now: the launch timing for the rocket, the 600 km altitude, and the claim that the satellite will be in constant sunlight, which I'm comparing against what the draft actually says about the solar panels.

I'm checking the orbit's RAAN requirement next, since a sun-synchronous orbit needs it to shift by a fixed amount each year, and the draft's wording on that is shaky. I'm also looking at the end-of-life manoeuvre claim, which contradicts the statement that the satellite has no thrusters, and the drag-sail sentence that stops short.

I'm checking the drag-sail sentence and the access table's duplicated entry next, and I'm about to pull a quote from the ground station section.

I'm checking the quoted text against the draft now, starting with the ground station claim that near-polar orbits need a polar site, which conflicts with the Tasmania choice. Next I'm pulling the wording around the "purposed" typo and the Wikipedia reference, to confirm both are quoted accurately.

I'm checking the Great Barrier Reef claims against the figures, which are just as shaky: the ocean acidity wording is roughly right, but the 2016 bleaching number needs a source. I'm also noting the STK 3D view caption has no figure number, and the orbit-path image labels are missing numbers too. Then there's the launch-date mismatch between the Vega E's 2024 debut and the 2025 dates in the access table.

I'm now checking the remaining claims: the access summary seems to cover only two days despite listing 15 passes, and the executive summary promises perturbation calculations that never appear in the work.
